title: Game Trees
body:
A [[Tree]] whose nodes are game positions and whose edges are legal moves. The root is the
position on the board now, the children are everything you could do about it, and a leaf is a
finished game. Playing well means searching it.

**This is not a [[Search Trees|search tree]].** A search tree encodes an *ordering* so that
lookup is a walk from the root; a game tree encodes *possibility* and nothing is sorted. The two
share the word "tree" and nothing else.

## Minimax

Two players want opposite things, so label the levels alternately: **MAX** picks the largest
child value, **MIN** picks the smallest. Score the leaves from MAX's point of view (win $+1$,
draw $0$, loss $-1$) and the values propagate back up:

```
             MAX          3        ← you play the move worth 3
            /   \
   MIN     3     2                 ← opponent takes your best line down
          / \   / \
   MAX   3   5 2   9               ← leaf scores
```

The value at the root is what the position is worth **assuming the opponent plays as well as you
do**. That assumption is the whole model: minimax is not predicting what the opponent will do, it
is refusing to hope. It is naturally [[Recursion|recursive]], one function that flips between
taking a max and a min at each level.

Solved games are the ones where this search actually finished. Tic-tac-toe is a draw, checkers is
a draw (proved 2007), chess and Go are not solved and will not be.

## Why it never finishes

With **branching factor** $b$ (legal moves per position) and **depth** $d$ (plies, one player's
move each), the tree has $O(b^d)$ leaves. See [[Time Complexity]].

| Game | $b$ | Full game tree |
|---|---|---|
| Tic-tac-toe | ~4 | ~$10^5$, searchable to the end |
| Checkers | ~8 | ~$10^{20}$ |
| Chess | ~35 | ~$10^{120}$ |
| Go | ~250 | ~$10^{360}$ |

$10^{120}$ is more positions than there are atoms in the observable universe, so the exhaustive
version of the algorithm is correct and useless. Everything below is a way of not looking at
most of the tree.

## Alpha-beta pruning

Carry two bounds down the search: $\alpha$, the best MAX can already guarantee, and $\beta$, the
best MIN can already guarantee. **The moment $\alpha \ge \beta$, stop expanding this node**, its
siblings cannot change the answer.

The reasoning is one sentence: if MIN has already found a reply here that is worse for MAX than
something MAX can get elsewhere, MAX will never come down this branch, so what the rest of it
contains does not matter. Alpha-beta returns **exactly the minimax value**, it is not an
approximation.

Payoff depends entirely on move ordering. With the best move tried first every time, the cost
falls from $O(b^d)$ to $O(b^{d/2})$: the same time buys **twice the depth**, or equivalently the
effective branching factor drops to $\sqrt{b}$. With random ordering you get about $O(b^{3d/4})$.
This is why real engines spend effort on ordering heuristics (try captures first, try the move
that worked at the previous depth) before spending it on anything else.

## Evaluation functions and the horizon

Since the search cannot reach real leaves, cut it off at a fixed depth and score the position
with a **static evaluation function**: material count, king safety, mobility, whatever the game
suggests. The tree is now a heuristic device rather than a proof.

Two consequences worth knowing by name:

- **The horizon effect.** A disaster one ply past the cutoff is invisible, so the engine will
  happily make pointless delaying moves to push it over the horizon. Fixed by *quiescence
  search*: keep going while captures and checks are pending, stop only in quiet positions.
- **Evaluation is where the knowledge lives.** Search depth is generic; the evaluation function
  is the part that knows what game is being played. Modern engines learn it instead of hand-tuning
  it, which is where this chapter meets [[Neural Network]] and [[MACHINE LEARNING]].

Games with chance (backgammon) add a third node type whose value is an expectation over the dice
rather than a max or a min, and alpha-beta stops working cleanly. Games with hidden information
(poker) break the model outright: there is no single position to sit at the root.

## Core facts

- Nodes are positions, edges are moves, leaves are finished games.
- Minimax assumes an optimal opponent; it is a worst-case guarantee, not a prediction.
- One ply is one player's move; "depth 6" in chess usually means 6 plies, not 6 full moves.
- The tree is $O(b^d)$, and for anything past checkers that number is unreachable.
- Alpha-beta prunes when $\alpha \ge \beta$ and gives **the same answer** as full minimax.
- Best case alpha-beta is $O(b^{d/2})$: good move ordering doubles the searchable depth.
- Cutting the search off requires a static evaluation function, and that is what introduces the
  horizon effect.
- Deep Blue searched; AlphaGo searched **and** learned the evaluation. Both are this tree.

---

This note **is** the adversarial-search block of [[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]], which links here
rather than writing its own. Two connections into the rest of that course: an evaluation function
is a [[Heuristic]] with no admissibility guarantee, which is what the horizon effect is a symptom
of; and minimax takes the **worst** case where [[Expected Utility]] takes the expected one,
because here the uncertainty is an opponent rather than a die.
